subject: Architecture
title: Persian Persepolis: Platform of Kings
description: One-minute skill: Persian Persepolis: Platform of Kings.

hook.text: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of an empire stretching from Egypt to India.

buildup.text: Darius the Great built it on a massive stone platform with staircases wide enough for horses to climb.

discovery.text: Carvings show 23 nations bringing tribute — each delegation wears distinct clothing and carries unique gifts.

twist.text: Alexander the Great burned Persepolis in 330 BC. Some historians say it was drunken revenge for Athens.

climax.text: Workers from across the empire built it together — Persepolis mixed Egyptian, Greek, and Babylonian styles.

punchline.text: An empire of many cultures built one palace. Then one man burned it.

details.summary: Persepolis was the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, built on a massive stone platform starting around 518 BCE. Its columned halls, carved staircases.
details.whyItMatters: Persepolis blended architectural styles from across the empire — Egyptian, Greek, Mesopotamian — into something new. It demonstrates how imperial architecture can synthesize conquered cultures into a unified statement of power.
takeaways: Persepolis was the Achaemenid Empire's ceremonial capital
Built on a stone platform starting around 518 BCE
Relief carvings depict 23 subject nations bringing tribute

faq.question: Why was Persepolis destroyed?
faq.answer: Alexander the Great burned Persepolis in 330 BCE, reportedly in revenge for the Persian burning of Athens. The fire destroyed the wooden roofs and upper structures, but the stone platform, columns, and relief carvings survived to be excavated millennia later.

faq.question: What made Persepolis architecturally unique?
faq.answer: It fused architectural elements from across the empire — Egyptian door frames, Greek-influenced columns, Mesopotamian platform construction — creating a deliberately cosmopolitan style. Workers and artists from across the empire contributed their traditions.
